newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Rubber to bounce as shortage forecast.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rubber to bounce as shortage forecast.

text.p: The world is heading for a shortage of natural rubber, a raw material for tyres, by the turn of the century as global demand exceeds exports from key growers, industry experts said.

The supply crunch could emerge as early as 2002 and the deficit would continue to widen as the big three producers -- Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia -- retained a greater share of their output for domestic consumption.

The experts, attending an international rubber meeting here, said the shortage implied that "in the long-term, the natural rubber price is likely to perform better than prices of many other commodities".
Natural rubber prices are now at three-year lows but economists say a rebound is on the cards.

Prices will rise further until the end of this century after which a global supply deficit will send the market surging, Hidde Smit, managing director of Amsterdam-based Economic and Social Institute, said.
He said at the meeting that the market was expected to absorb at attractive prices 7.5 million tonnes of natural rubber by year 2000 and 11 million by 2020.
"A price of four Singapore dollars 10 years from now is possible," he said. The price is now at below $2 a kg.
Natural rubber's greatest competitor is synthetic rubber produced from oil and chemicals but both are used in tyre production, which consumes most of the world's rubber.
The United States, Europe and Japan are the biggest users of elastomer -- encompassing both natural and synthetic rubber.
World demand for elastomer has expanded by an average of 3.6 percent a year in the past 36 years to reach 16 million tonnes in 1996.
The natural rubber demand alone is expected to grow by an average of 3.5 percent a year after the year 2000, said the International Rubber Study Group (IRSG), which is hosting this week's event.
Consumption stood at 6.3 million tonnes in 1996 and this is expected to grow by 200,000 tonnes this year.
"As demand continues to increase while supply declines, natural rubber consumers will eventually face shortages," the IRSG said in its latest market report.
The centre of gravity for rubber is the Asia-Pacific region which is experiencing a rapid growth in car and tyre demand, IRSG officials said.
But natural rubber production in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia could stagnate as they become more industrialised.

Prachaya Jumpasut, chief economist at the IRSG, said the industrialisation in the three largest producers implied a shift by the three from being predominantly rubber exporters to their retaining a greater proportion of their production for domestic use.
Hence there will probably be "a declining volume of rubber available for export to the world markets".

Rubber prices have fallen to 36-month lows due to the unseasonal rise in southeast Asian production, a strike at Goodyear in the U.S, slow Chinese demand and the release of stockpiled rubber by the United States.
The depressed prices have forced the Thai government to inteverne in the local market to help prop up farm prices.
Some smallholders in Malaysia have abandoned rubber and have turned to growing tobacco or orchard fruits.
A.F.S. Bufiman, executive director of the Indonesian Rubber Association, said the current Indonesian price of 48 U.S. cents per lb was well below production cost.
